B1.title: The effect of IL-4 on the expression of TAS2R bitter taste receptors in human peripheral blood monocytes and lymphocytes in vitro
B1.journal: Bulletin Physiology and Pathology of Respiration
B1.abstract:
Introduction. 
                    Interleukin-4 (IL-4) is a key mediator of Th2 inflammation in asthma and is capable of profoundly altering the receptor profile of monocytes. However, data on the effect of IL-4 on the expression of the bitter taste receptor family (TAS2R) in circulating immune cells are currently lacking.
                   
                   
                        Aim. 
                    To characterize the effect of recombinant IL-4 at physiologically and pathophysiologically relevant concentrations on the protein expression of TAS2R4, TAS2R5, TAS2R14, TAS2R20, TAS2R31, and TAS2R38 in subsets of monocytes and lymphocytes from the peripheral blood of healthy donors in vitro.
                   
                   
                        Materials and methods. 
                    The study was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 10 healthy volunteers. The cells were incubated for 24 hours with recombinant IL-4 at concentrations of 0.1, 1, and 10 ng/ml. TAS2R expression was assessed by flow cytometry on a FACSCanto II with analysis of the proportion of TAS2R-positive cells and normalized median fluorescence intensity (nMFI). Page's test and Wilcoxon's test for related samples were used for statistical processing.
                   
                   
                        Results. 
                    Under control conditions, all six studied receptors were detected in both monocytes and lymphocytes; however, their basal expression was significantly higher in monocytes. IL-4 exerted a pronounced dose-dependent inhibitory effect on TAS2R expression predominantly in monocytes. A monotonic downward trend was found for TAS2R4, TAS2R5, TAS2R14, and TAS2R38, while no significant changes were observed for TAS2R31. The most pronounced decrease in nMFI in monocytes was observed for TAS2R38, TAS2R14, and TAS2R5. TAS2R20 exhibited a biphasic response: an increase in the proportion of monocytes expressing TAS2R20 at the minimum dose of IL-4 was combined with a decrease in nMFI at 10 ng/ml. In lymphocytes, the effect of IL-4 was much less pronounced. Despite the presence of individual statistical trends, no biologically significant changes in TAS2R expressionwere detected.
                   
                   
                        Conclusion. 
                    In a pilot in vitro experiment, IL-4 was associated with a monotonic decrease in TAS2R expression in peripheral blood monocytes, with relative stability of TAS2R31 and minimal effect in lymphocytes. These data expand our understanding of the subpopulation- and receptor-specific influence of the Th2 cytokine environment on TAS2R-dependent immunoregulation and suggest that IL-4 may be a potential factor in reducing the chemosensory and antimicrobial readiness of myeloid cells in asthma.

B1.title:
Long-Chain Fatty
Acids Inhibit the Human Bitter Taste
Receptor TAS2R16 in a Structure-Dependent Manner
B1.journal:
Journal of Agricultural
and Food Chemistry
B1.abstract:
Abstract 
                   Bitterness limits the development of palatable foods containing bioactive ingredients. This study investigated whether long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) modulate the human bitter taste receptor TAS2R16 using a HEK293T cell-based calcium assay with salicin as an agonist. None of the tested LCFAs directly activated TAS2R16. Under co-treatment, only oleic acid inhibited salicin-induced calcium responses, shifting the salicin EC50 from 1.82 ± 0.11 mM to 3.55 ± 1.22 mM at 30 μM (p &lt; 0.01). Pretreatment with all LCFAs inhibited TAS2R16 concentration-dependently. Reliable IC50 values were obtained for palmitic acid (8.67 ± 1.44 μM), stearic acid (0.082 ± 0.002 μM), and oleic acid (0.41 ± 0.12 μM), whereas lower plateaus were not reached for myristic, linoleic, and α-linolenic acids. LCFA treatment did not consistently change membrane fluidity, and inhibition was attenuated in the TAS2R16 N96T mutant. These findings demonstrate compound- and treatment-dependent modulation of TAS2R16 by food-derived LCFAs.

B1.title: Bitter 2,5‐Diketopiperazines From Cocoa Activate Human Bitter Taste Receptors
B1.abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    The human taste system enables a rapid analysis of nutritional and non‐nutritional food constituents. Although a bitter taste is considered a warning signal against ingesting potentially harmful substances, not all bitter substances are toxic, and a moderate bitterness is frequently tolerated or even preferred. Responsible for the detection of bitter substances in food are the ∼25 human bitter taste receptors residing in the oral cavity. An important class of bitter compounds found in thermally treated foods is the 2,5‐diketopiperazines, cyclic dipeptides made from two L‐amino acids, which are frequently formed as degradation products of polypeptides. Although 2,5‐diketopiperazines are established as major contributors to the bitter taste of many food items, it is still unknown which of the human bitter taste receptors mediate their detection. Using functional calcium‐mobilization assays, we identified two human bitter taste receptors, TAS2R14 and TAS2R43, being responsive to 2,5‐diketopiperazines. Of the two identified 2,5‐diketopiperazines activating TAS2R43,
                     cis 
                    ‐cyclo(L‐Leu‐L‐Phe) exhibited the highest potency with a threshold concentration of 100 µM. Further testing of 2,5‐diketopiperazine‐related linear dipeptides revealed that 2,5‐diketopiperazines represent their own class of bitter compounds, as no overlapping activation patterns with the corresponding dipeptides were evident.

A1.title: Hydrogen-rich saline alleviates inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors in mice
A1.abstract: Despite the crucial role of inflammation in depression-like behavior, the low blood-brain barrier penetration of existing anti-inflammatory agents presents a substantial obstacle to effective treatment. Owing to the excellent blood-brain barrier permeability and anti-inflammatory ability of hydrogen-rich saline, this study explores its therapeutic effects on lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behavior in mice. In this study, mice intraperitoneally received lipopolysaccharide (0.83 mg/kg). Thirty minutes later, they intraperitoneally received hydrogen-rich saline (5 mL/kg). Results showed that hydrogen-rich saline significantly alleviated anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in lipopolysaccharide-treated mice, as assessed by open field tests, elevated plus maze tests, forced swim tests, and the tail suspension test. Peripheral inflammation was significantly reduced, associated with inhibited splenomegaly and decreased serum levels of interleukin-1β and tumor necrosis factor-α. Central inflammation was also decreased, related to the reduced number of activated microglia, inhibition of Tolllike receptor 4/myeloid differentiation primary response 88/nuclear factor-κB signaling, and repaired synaptic damage in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that early hydrogen-rich saline administration may attenuate lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors, at least in part, by suppressing microglial pro-inflammatory activation and Tolllike receptor 4/nuclear factor-κB signaling.

A1.title: Adaptation of DECIDE, a Shared Decision Making Intervention, to Improve Perinatal Mental Health Care in Health Systems
A1.abstract: Effectively engaging and communicating with perinatal individuals is crucial in meeting the unique decision needs of perinatal individuals, particularly those with anxiety, depression, or other mental health disorders. This study adapted DECIDE, a shared decision making intervention proven to be effective in behavioral health care for adults with psychiatric disorders. The adaptation was to improve perinatal care providers' competency in patient engagement and communication in health systems' perinatal care delivery. In this paper, we report on the adaptation strategies and processes for embedding DECIDE provider training into perinatal health and mental health care delivery. The Iterative Decision-making for Evaluation of Adaptation (IDEA) and the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications-Enhanced (FRAME) guided the adaptation of the DECIDE provider training. The adaptation of the DECIDE provider training was conducted in four phases: (1) conducting a literature review of empirical evidence, (2) engaging perinatal health and mental health care providers and content experts, (3) identifying and making specific content adaptations and developing clinical vignettes to fit perinatal care settings, and (4) recording the adapted training and new video illustrations and launching the adapted DECIDE for MOM provider training. The adaptation process engaged perinatal mental health and healthcare providers and experts in health systems as well as those who were part of the original DECIDE development and implementation team. After the two rounds of feedback, revision and consensus process, we finalized the training content, created clinical vignettes and filmed case illustrations based on the vignettes. After the iterative editing process of recorded modules and case illustration videos, the finalized DECIDE for MOM provider training was launched on Canvas in August 2025. The next step is to conduct feasibility evaluation of the adapted training by implementing the DECIDE for MOM provider training in health systems.

A1.title: Concordance and validity of federated versus centralized analyses in treatment-resistant depression
A1.abstract: To evaluate whether federated analyses can reproduce centralized results for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) risk prediction using privacy-preserving statistical models. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 7272 adults with incident major depressive disorder initiating antidepressants (2015-2021) in Maccabi Healthcare Services, Israel. Treatment-resistant depression was defined as progression to third-line regimens within 24 months. Data were geographically partitioned into 2 nodes to simulate federation. Federated generalized linear and Cox models were estimated using privacy-preserving iteratively reweighted least squares with cross-validated feature selection. Agreement with centralized analyses was assessed using coefficient differences, statistical-significance concordance, and confidence interval (CI) overlap. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination, calibration, and fairness metrics. Federated and centralized models showed near-perfect concordance. Feature selection produced almost identical predictor sets, and coefficient estimates were strongly aligned, with mean absolute differences <0.01, complete decision agreement among predictors retained by both models, and >95% CI overlap. Predictive performance was modest but consistent across settings (AUC ∼0.65 for logistic; ∼0.62 for Cox), with preserved calibration and similar subgroup patterns. Federated models reproduced major clinical associations observed centrally, including higher TRD risk with prior antidepressant exposure, psychiatric hospitalization, anxiety and personality disorders, and polypharmacy, and lower risk with atrial fibrillation and delayed therapy initiation. Results show that federated implementations of standard epidemiologic models can retain the validity and stability of centralized analyses, even for complex psychiatric outcomes requiring high-dimensional adjustment. Federated analysis can closely replicate centralized statistical model results while preserving privacy, supporting its use for scalable, multi-institutional epidemiologic research.

A1.title: Dynamic associations between received social support, PTSD, and depressive symptoms during post-burn recovery
A1.abstract: Background: Social support is an important determinant of psychological adjustment following trauma, yet its temporal relationship with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depressive symptoms remains incompletely understood among burn survivors. The present study examined the dynamic associations between received social support, PTSD symptoms, and depressive symptoms during the first two years following burn injury.Method: A total of 118 adult burn patients were recruited from the largest burn centre in Taiwan. Received social support, PTSD symptoms, and depressive symptoms were assessed at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-burn. Four-wave cross-lagged panel analyses were conducted to examine longitudinal associations among these variables.Results: Higher levels of received social support at 3 months predicted lower PTSD symptoms and depressive symptoms at 6 months. In contrast, higher depressive symptoms at 12 months predicted lower received social support at 24 months. No significant associations were observed between PTSD symptoms and subsequent social support.Conclusions: Early received social support may promote psychological adjustment following burn injury, whereas persistent depressive symptoms may contribute to later reductions in social support.

A1.title: The Natural History of Spinocerebellar Ataxia Types 7 and 8
A1.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxias are genetically heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive cerebellar degeneration. Among them, SCA7 and SCA8 are particularly rare, and their longitudinal natural history has not been well defined. Using data from the Clinical Research Consortium for the Study of Cerebellar Ataxias, we examined disease progression in genetically confirmed SCA7 and SCA8 patients in North America. Longitudinal changes in motor severity were assessed using the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA), alongside cognitive function (Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome scale [CCAS]) and depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)), applying linear mixed-effects models with genetic and clinical covariates. Our cohort included 27 individuals with SCA7 and 51 with SCA8 with baseline data, among which 22 individuals with SCA7 and 42 with SCA8 have longitudinal follow-up. Age at onset in SCA7 was inversely associated with pathologic repeat length (β = -1.43, p < 0.01), whereas no significant correlation was observed in SCA8 (β = -0.08, p = 0.28). Longitudinal analyses demonstrated that SCA7 progressed relatively rapidly, with SARA scores worsening by 1.68 points per year, while SCA8 showed substantially slower progression at 0.47 points per year. In both disorders, progression was predominantly driven by deterioration in the axial SARA domain, particularly gait and stance. In contrast, CCAS and PHQ-9 scores remained stable over approximately 5 years of follow-up, with no significant longitudinal changes detected. These findings demonstrate distinct disease trajectories between SCA7 and SCA8 to inform future longitudinal studies and therapeutic trials.

A1.title: Urban heat radiation and health perception in Addis Ababa
A1.abstract: Exposure to high temperatures poses a multidimensional health hazard. Low- and middle-income countries are likely to experience large increases in average annual temperature due to climate change. Ethiopia is expected to warm by up to 4 °C by 2100. We investigated the association between land surface temperature (LST) and health-related quality of life (HRQOL). This is, to our knowledge, one of the first studies of its kind to be conducted in a large African urban cohort. We analyzed cross-sectional data from the COMBAT cohort in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, collected in January 2025 (N = 3201). HRQOL was assessed using the EQ-5D-5L; the outcome variables were the utility index and its five dimensions. LST exposure was characterized using baseline and proximal metrics. We used a beta-one-inflated regression and logistic regression to assess associations. Overall, 53.6% of participants reported problems in at least one EQ-5D-5L dimension, with anxiety or depression being the most frequent (33.5%). Individuals reporting problems were exposed to a slightly higher median baseline LST (32.73 vs. 32.43 °C). We observed a consistent inverted U-shaped association between LST and the probability of reporting perfect health. The probability of reporting problems increased at higher LST values in usual activities, self-care, and anxiety or depression. The results suggest that deviations from the local thermal average are negatively associated with perceived health. This study illustrates the potential value of integrating HRQOL indicators into public health surveillance to enable timely intervention against the health impacts of climate change.

A1.title: Identifying characteristics and behavioral phenotypes of musculoskeletal disorders using wearables in All of Us
A1.abstract: Wearable devices provide continuous measures of daily activity, sleep, and heart-rate (HR)-derived characteristics, creating new opportunities for digital phenotyping of musculoskeletal disorders (MSD). However, longitudinal behavioral patterns and heterogeneity among individuals with MSD remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify characteristics associated with MSD and characterize behavioral phenotypes using longitudinal wearable data. We analyzed 2344 participants (MSD = 1036; non-MSD = 1308) from the All of Us Research Program. First, supervised machine-learning models were trained using sociodemographic, physical measurement, and wearable-derived features to distinguish individuals with and without MSD and identify factors associated with MSD status. Model interpretation was performed using SHapley Additive exPlanations values. Second, temporal profiling and unsupervised clustering were applied to 90-day wearable trajectories of participants with MSD to identify behavioral phenotypes. XGBoost achieved the best classification performance (accuracy = 0.929, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve = 0.930, area under the precision-recall curve = 0.870, F1 = 0.919). Important factors associated with MSD included lower activity, longer sleep, and female sex. Behavioral phenotyping identified 5 distinct phenotypes differing in activity patterns, sleep characteristics, HR-derived measures, pain burden, mental health conditions, and employment status. Notably, high-pain phenotypes exhibited greater prevalence of anxiety and depressive disorders, lower pulse rate variability, and distinct sleep profiles compared with more active phenotypes. These phenotypes demonstrated moderate reproducibility in bootstrap-based stability analysis (mean adjusted rand index = 0.62). Longitudinal wearable data revealed behavioral heterogeneity among individuals with MSD that was not fully explained by traditional diagnostic categories. These findings demonstrate the value of wearable-based digital phenotyping for characterizing differences in daily functioning and symptom burden among individuals with MSD. Wearable-derived behavioral phenotyping provides a complementary approach for understanding heterogeneity in MSD and may support future efforts in patient monitoring, stratification, and personalized management.

A1.title: Do specific cancer types show higher expression of depression and anxiety linked genes? A transparent computational study
A1.abstract: Depression and anxiety are common in people with cancer, but whether some cancers show higher expression of genes linked to these conditions remains unclear. We analysed genetic studies to examine whether this molecular burden differs across cancers after accounting for normal tissue. We used strong genome-wide association findings for diagnosis-level major depression and anxiety disorders to select genes mapped to associated genetic regions. Tumor expression was compared separately with the cancer genome atlas (TCGA) adjacent normals and genotype-tissue expression (GTEx) healthy tissue. Same-donor GTEx samples were combined. We checked uncertainty and changes in results across analyses, then explored gene relationships, biological pathways and protein connections. Stomach adenocarcinoma showed consistent positive burden versus GTEx (+ 0.718, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.558-0.939) and TCGA normals (+ 0.225, 95% CI 0.090-0.423). Lower-grade glioma was also elevated versus normal brain (+ 0.471, 95% CI 0.407-0.545). Esophageal carcinoma was elevated versus GTEx (+ 0.799, 95% CI 0.653-1.037) but not TCGA normals. Glioblastoma and testicular germ-cell tumor were not elevated after tissue adjustment. Exploratory Elastic Net suggested a pattern across many genes. Most pathway tests were not significant after correction. Within-panel Polycomb repressive complex enrichment remained significant (q = 0.0319). Some cancers express genes linked to depression or anxiety in genetic studies more strongly than their normal tissues; others show smaller or tissue-dependent differences. The findings suggest that this molecular pattern varies across cancer types and is distributed across many genes, with more limited evidence for shared pathways or closely connected gene networks.

A1.title: Intelligent control of spreading depression in a dual-layer ring network under saturation constraints
A1.abstract: Spreading depression (SD) is a phenomenon characterized by complete depolarization of neurons and glial cells, and is associated with various brain disorders such as migraine and stroke. The initiation and propagation of SD are regulated by multiple factors, exhibiting typical nonlinear characteristics. Pharmacological options for SD-related disorders remain limited by efficacy, tolerability, and safety concerns. This situation has motivated computational investigation of non-pharmacological, closed-loop neuromodulation strategies. Based on the Wei model and a double-layer ring network model, this paper proposes an intelligent control framework with predictive capability and saturation constraints. Firstly, a temporal convolutional network (TCN) is constructed to predict extracellular potassium concentration, which is then used to identify potential SD events. Next, a controller with saturation constraints is designed based on a radial basis function (RBF) neural network to address the identified SD. When SD is about to occur, real-time intervention is achieved through a cyclic process of prediction-identification-regulation. Simulation results show that the proposed framework can identify impending SD and suppress its initiation and propagation under bounded stimulation amplitudes. These in silico findings provide a computational basis for further study of closed-loop neuromodulation for SD-related disorders.

B2.title: The Oral Microbiota–Taste Axis: Microbial Influences on Gustatory Perception and Food Sensory Experience
B2.abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   Taste is a key determinant of food choice and dietary behavior, yet differences in taste perception are often attributed mainly to genetic variation, taste receptor expression, and neural processing. Emerging evidence suggests that the oral microbiota may represent an additional, and largely overlooked, factor influencing gustatory perception. This review examines the potential role of oral microorganisms in shaping taste by bringing together current evidence from oral microbiology, taste physiology, and nutritional science. Particular attention is given to the close association between tongue‐associated microbial communities and taste buds, and to the potential effects of microbial biofilms, local pH changes, and microbial metabolites on the chemical environment surrounding taste receptors. The review further considers how these interactions may influence taste sensitivity, food preferences, dietary patterns, and, ultimately, metabolic health. Importantly, current evidence remains largely associative, and direct mechanistic links between specific microorganisms, microbial metabolites, and taste receptor function are still poorly defined. We therefore highlight key methodological and knowledge gaps and discuss emerging opportunities for dietary modulation, oral probiotics, and microbiome‐informed approaches. Understanding this oral microbiota–taste axis may provide a new perspective on taste variability and its nutritional consequences.

B2.title: From Taste Perception to Metabolic Regulation: Associations Among Taste Sensitivity, Taste- and Metabolic Trait-Related Genes, Body Composition and Lipid Mediator Signaling in a Human Exploratory Study
B2.abstract: Background/Objectives: Taste sensitivity has been associated with body mass index (BMI) independently of dietary intake, suggesting that taste-related pathways may influence metabolic health beyond food consumption. However, the mechanisms underlying these associations remain unclear. We investigated relationships among taste-related and metabolically relevant single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), body composition, red blood cell (RBC) total lipids, fatty acids (FAs), and lipid mediators to identify potential associations between taste perception and metabolic phenotype. Methods: Body composition, RBC total lipids, FAs, and N-acylethanolamines (NAEs) were assessed in 52 healthy subjects genotyped for selected SNPs in taste-related genes (TAS1R2, TAS1R3, GNAT3, CD36), and genes involved in nutrient-sensing NAE metabolism (FGF21, FAAH and PPARα). The associations were evaluated using explanatory univariate analyses and regression models. Results: Carriers of the GNAT3 rs7792845 CC genotype showed a lower mean fat-free mass percentage and higher RBC total lipids than carriers of the CT genotype. CD36 rs1761667 and rs1984112 were associated with NAE lipid mediators and rs1761667 with RBC total lipids, with AA genotype carriers showing higher mean values. Regression analyses identified GNAT3 rs7792845, FGF21 rs838133, and taste-sensitivity scores associated with body composition, accounting for 41.5% of the variance, and CD36 rs1761667 and rs1984112 associated with lipid and NAE values, accounting for up to 38.1% of the variance. FAAH rs324420 and TAS1R2 rs35874116 were involved in RBG lipid and NAE models. The specific lipid species underlying these associations remain unknown. Conclusions: These findings suggest that sensory- and nutrient-sensing pathways might contribute to interindividual variability in metabolic phenotypes.

B2.title: Evaluation of taste-based school–home collaborative nutrition education on taste perception and eating behaviors among Japanese schoolchildren
B2.abstract:
Background 
                     Taste perception plays a key role in shaping children's food choices and eating behaviors. 
                   
                   
                     Aim 
                     This exploratory quasi-experimental study aimed to examine the effects of a taste-based, school–home collaborative nutrition education program on children's taste perception and eating behaviors. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     
                      This study involved 64 fourth- and fifth-grade children and their parents who were assigned to either the intervention (
                       n 
                       = 32) or control (
                       n 
                       = 32) groups. For 6 months, the intervention group received newsletters about taste, healthy food, and dietary intake, as well as taste test results and individualized feedback on their dietary intake. The control group did not receive any intervention. We collected data on children's taste perception, eating behaviors, self-efficacy, dietary intake, and parental healthy eating literacy pre- and post-intervention. Abstract

C3.title: Microglia coordinate circadian regulation of glymphatic brain clearance in neuroimmune disease: a conceptual framework
C3.abstract:
Abstract 
                   The glymphatic system is a brain-wide fluid and solute transport pathway that contributes to cerebrospinal fluid-interstitial fluid exchange and the removal of metabolites, inflammatory mediators, and aggregation-prone proteins. Glymphatic activity is shaped by sleep state, vascular pulsatility, respiration, vasomotion, astrocytic aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarization, meningeal lymphatic drainage, and circadian timing. However, key aspects of brain fluid transport remain debated, including the relative roles of perivascular spaces, periarterial basement membrane pathways, intramural periarterial drainage, diffusion, convection, and anesthesia-dependent physiology. These uncertainties are central to neuroimmune disease, where inflammation, sleep disruption, vascular dysfunction, astrocytic disorganization, and microglial state changes frequently coexist. Here, we review evidence that microglia may coordinate circadian regulation of glymphatic brain clearance. Microglia are circadian, purinergic, and morphologically dynamic immune cells positioned near synapses, vessels, astrocytes, and perivascular spaces. Microglial activity appears to be temporally coupled to physiological states and clearance pathways relevant to glymphatic function: microglial surveillance varies across natural sleep-wake states, microglial phagocytosis can compensate for impaired AQP4-dependent clearance, and meningeal lymphatic drainage shapes microglial inflammatory responses. Recent work further shows that microglial morphology, signaling through the P2Y12 receptor (encoded by P2RY12), and glymphatic tracer influx are linked across Zeitgeber time, and that acute P2Y12 blockade can phase-shift glymphatic rhythms and alter sleep architecture. We propose that microglia may act as neuroimmune chronomodulators that influence the timing and spatial organization of clearance rather than as simple enhancers or inhibitors of flow; however, microglial changes may also represent adaptive responses to altered sleep, vascular physiology, astrocytic state, or glymphatic transport. In neuroimmune disease, glymphatic dysfunction may reflect temporal misalignment among microglial state, sleep architecture, vascular dynamics, astrocytic AQP4 polarity, and fluid transport routes. This framework supports temporally resolved experimental designs and translational studies integrating glymphatic imaging, sleep physiology, circadian biomarkers, inflammatory markers, vascular measures, and cognitive outcomes.

C3.title: Neuroimmune regulation of visceral pain: roles of microglia, purinergic signaling, and neuroinflammation
C3.abstract: Visceral hypersensitivity is a hallmark pathophysiological feature of irritable bowel syndrome, characterized by enhanced perception of visceral stimuli and a reduced pain threshold. Although previous studies have mainly attributed visceral hypersensitivity to peripheral inflammation, visceral afferent sensitization, and psychological stress, these mechanisms do not fully explain the persistent pain and discomfort observed in some patients without overt organic lesions or pronounced inflammation. Accumulating evidence indicates that the spinal cord is not merely a relay site for visceral sensory afferent input, but also a critical central locus for pain modulation and amplification. As resident immune cells of the central nervous system, spinal microglia can be activated by persistent visceral stimulation, inflammation, and stress, thereby contributing to the development and maintenance of visceral hypersensitivity through neuroimmune crosstalk. This review summarizes the role of spinal microglia in the development and progression of visceral hypersensitivity and the associated molecular mechanisms. For the first time in this research field, a two-dimensional reaction-diffusion numerical model was established using COMSOL Multiphysics to simulate the spatiotemporal diffusion and degradation patterns of key signaling molecules, including CSF1, ATP, and BDNF, within the microenvironment of the spinal dorsal horn. The model further incorporates coupled analyses of dynamic changes in microglial activation states and neuronal membrane responses, providing a theoretical basis for quantitatively elucidating microglia-mediated pain sensitization. Evidence indicates that signaling molecules such as ATP, CX3CL1, and CSF1 can drive the activation of microglia in the spinal dorsal horn and induce the release of mediators including TNF-α, IL-1β, and BDNF. These changes enhance excitatory synaptic transmission, weaken inhibitory neurotransmission, and promote spinal and central sensitization. Among these mechanisms, the BDNF-TrkB-KCC2/NMDAR signaling axis represents a key molecular pathway underlying microglia-mediated pain amplification. Furthermore, peripheral factors, including intestinal inflammation, psychological stress, and gut microbiota dysbiosis, may further regulate spinal microglial reactivity through the gut-brain axis, thereby exacerbating visceral hypersensitivity. This review not only summarizes recent advances in understanding the involvement of spinal microglia in visceral hypersensitivity, but also provides a theoretical basis for mechanistic studies and targeted interventions in other neuroinflammation-related pathological processes and chronic pain disorders.

C3.title: Abstract 65: Neuroimmune Crosstalk Drives Microglia-Dependent Neuronal Dysfunction in Hypertension

Background: 
                    Neuroimmune activation in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus contributes to sympathetic overactivity and neurogenic hypertension. Microglia are key regulators of this response, but the receptor-specific mechanisms that convert microglial activation into neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. The kinin B1 receptor (B1R) is induced during inflammation and can promote mitochondrial oxidative stress, while Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) promotes innate immune activation and NLRP3 inflammasome priming. Because mitochondrial stress can provide a secondary signal for inflammasome activation, we hypothesized that B1R-TLR4 crosstalk drives microglial inflammatory activation and downstream neuronal dysfunction in neurogenic hypertension.
                   
                   
                     Methods: 
                    Mice received Angiotensin II (Ang II, 600 ng/kg/min) with vehicle, B1R antagonist (SSR240612, 5 mg/kg/day), TLR4 inhibitor (TAK-242, 3 mg/kg/day), or dual blockade for 28 days. Primary microglia were treated with LPS and/or LDABK with or without blockade of B1R, TLR4, or NLRP3 (MCC950). Microglia to neuron signaling was assessed using conditioned media, transwell co-culture, and direct co-cultures of neurons and microglia.
                   
                   
                     Results: 
                    Ang II increased B1R-TLR4 interactions in the PVN, with signal predominately in microglia, as indicated by proximity ligation assay. B1R or TLR4 blockade attenuated systolic blood pressure, whereas dual inhibition reduced pressure to near-control levels (Ang II: 166 ± 6; SSR240612: 154 ± 3; TAK-242: 158 ± 4; dual blockade: 143 ± 3; saline: 140 ± 1 mmHg). Given the localization of B1R-TLR4 to microglia, we investigated underlying mechanisms using primary microglia cultures. B1R activation alone increased mitochondrial oxidative stress, calcium accumulation, and altered membrane potential without NLRP3 activation. TLR4 priming prior to B1R activation further induced mitochondrial dysfunction and increased NLRP3, caspase-1, and IL-1β. B1R or TLR4 blockade reduced these responses. MCC950 eliminated NLRP3 activation but failed to rescue mitochondrial dysfunction, confirming NLRP3 as a downstream effector of B1R-TLR4 signaling. To determine if neuronal dysfunction results from direct B1R-TLR4 activation or secondary from microglia, neurons were exposed to activated microglia through conditioned media, transwell, or direct co-culture. Direct neuronal responses were minimal, whereas microglia-neuron communication produced greater neuronal mitochondrial stress and inflammasome activation, with the strongest effects observed in direct co-culture.
                   
                   
                     Conclusion: 
                    These findings identify B1R-TLR4 crosstalk as a neuroimmune mechanism driving elevated blood pressure, microglial inflammatory activation, and secondary neuronal dysfunction. Targeting this pathway may disrupt microglia-to-neuron inflammatory signaling in neurogenic hypertension.

C1.title: Modulation of neuroimmunity by early-life microbiota colonization
C1.abstract: Early life (fetal period to 2-3 y postnatally) is a critical window for the coordinated development of the intestine, lungs, and brain. As core pathways mediating microbe-immune-neuron crosstalk, the gut-brain and lung-brain axes drive cross-organ communication via early-life microbiota colonization, profoundly shaping immune maturation and neurodevelopmental trajectories. During fetal development, maternal microbial metabolites cross the placenta to prime in utero immune and neural development. After birth, rapid microbial colonization occurs in the intestine and lungs. Through signaling molecules including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan metabolites, and bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs), coupled with vagal nerve and mucosal immune pathways, the microbiota maintains intestinal and pulmonary immune homeostasis, preserves blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and modulates microglial activation, thereby regulating neurogenesis, synaptic pruning, and brain functional programming. Early-life dysbiosis is commonly associated with preterm birth, cesarean delivery, infection, and antibiotic exposure. In human observational studies, it accompanies disrupted organ homeostasis and neuroinflammatory signatures, and is linked to an increased long-term risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability; in neonatal animal models, it aggravates hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and encephalopathy of prematurity. Because dysbiosis frequently co-occurs with prematurity, infection, and other confounders, these associations do not by themselves establish causality. This review summarizes early-life colonization patterns of intestinal and pulmonary microbiota and their underlying neuroimmune mechanisms, analyzes the impacts of dysbiosis on neuroimmunity and related diseases, and proposes intervention strategies, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for neonatal health protection and neurodevelopmental disorder prevention.

C1.title: An Anti-Adhesive Hydrogel Delivering Ginger-Derived Exosome-Like Nanoparticles Reshapes the Neuroinflammatory Microenvironment After Traumatic Brain Injury
C1.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers secondary injury involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, highlighting the need for multi-target therapies. Ginger-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (GELNs) offer multi-target therapeutic potential but are limited by insufficient local retention and rapid clearance. TBI-induced brain-skull adhesion may further aggravate the pathological environment. To address these limitations, an anti-adhesive hydrogel (CG) composed of methacrylated chondroitin sulfate and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine is loaded with GELNs to form CG-GELNs. CG-GELNs attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion and provides greater behavioral benefits than free GELNs, including reduced anxiety-like behavior, improved social novelty discrimination, and enhanced spatial memory. At the pathological level, CG-GELNs confers coordinated protection against secondary injury by preserving blood-brain barrier integrity, suppressing pro-inflammatory responses, mitigating mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, and ultimately preserving synaptic function. Mechanistically, GELNs-associated microRNA-396 (miR-396) suppresses secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) expression, and functional rescue experiments support the contribution of this miR-396/SPP1 axis to the anti-inflammatory effects of GELNs in microglial cells. Overall, CG-GELNs simultaneously improves localized delivery of GELNs, attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion, and suppresses neuroinflammation, offering a potentially translatable therapeutic platform for remodeling the neuroinflammatory microenvironment and promoting neurological recovery after TBI.

C1.abstract: Diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) relies on subjective criteria and lacks objective biomarkers. Serum extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry stable cargo and can cross the blood-brain barrier, making them attractive biomarker sources. We therefore profiled serum EVs from a discovery cohort of 60 participants (40 healthy controls [HCs], 20 MDD patients) by size-exclusion chromatography and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and subsequently validated candidate proteins by ELISA in an independent cohort of 60 participants (20 HCs, 20 MDD, 20 patients with schizophrenia [SCZ]). In addition, a logistic-regression model combining EV-associated APLP1, TF and TNC distinguished MDD from HCs with an area under the curve of 0.905 (95% CI 0.812-0.998; 0.830 by leave-one-out cross-validation), outperforming individual proteins (TF 0.725; TNC 0.758; APLP1 0.725). Collectively, these findings define a serum EV-associated proteomic signature in MDD and preliminarily validate TF, TNC and APLP1 as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, implicating immune-inflammatory and complement-related pathways. C1.title: Modernizing reporting and communication of isolated echogenic intracardiac foci and choroid plexus cysts in the cell-free DNA era
C1.abstract: Echogenic intracardiac foci and choroid plexus cysts are among the most common findings on second-trimester prenatal ultrasound. Historically classified as "soft markers," they were incorporated into aneuploidy risk assessment in an era when screening relied on maternal age and serum analytes with limited performance. The widespread adoption of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening has fundamentally altered this paradigm. With detection rates exceeding 99% for trisomy 21, the modest likelihood ratios associated with isolated EIF and CPC no longer meaningfully alter post-test probability or clinical management. These findings are therefore best regarded as common normal variants rather than clinically significant markers of aneuploidy. Despite this transformation in prenatal screening, reporting and communication practices have changed little and remain highly variable, often influenced by historical practice patterns and medicolegal concerns rather than contemporary evidence. Numerous studies demonstrate that disclosure of isolated EIF and CPC may result in maternal anxiety, persistent concern despite reassurance, unnecessary diagnostic testing, and disruption of maternal-fetal bonding. These effects may be amplified by immediate patient access to ultrasound reports and terminology that continues to imply pathology where none exists. This review examines the historical and contemporary evidence supporting a modernized approach to the reporting and communication of isolated EIF and CPC in the era of cfDNA screening and proposes an evidence-based framework for clinical practice. In pregnancies with low-risk cfDNA results and a normal detailed fetal anatomic survey, isolated EIF and CPCs should be regarded as benign findings without clinical significance. Contemporary evidence no longer supports the routine reporting and communication of these findings in the context of aneuploidy risk. When disclosure occurs, communication should be non-alarmist, emphasize that these are normal variants, and avoid terminology suggesting increased risk for chromosomal abnormalities. Aligning reporting and communication with current evidence has the potential to reduce patient harm while promoting patient-centered prenatal care.

C1.title: Beyond weakness: The overlooked cognitive face of myasthenia gravis
C1.abstract: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease mediated by autoantibodies. Traditionally, it was strictly defined as a neuromuscular junction-specific disorder, believed not to affect the central nervous system (CNS). However, recent clinical observations and neuropsychological studies have demonstrated that a significant proportion of MG patients exhibit cognitive dysfunction, with clinical manifestations encompassing impairments in multiple cognitive domains such as verbal fluency, information processing speed, and memory. Neuroimaging further reveals structural and functional alterations in MG patients, including gray matter volume atrophy and abnormalities in default mode network connectivity. These findings challenge previous cognitive frameworks, suggesting that the disease may exert broader effects on the CNS. Current understanding indicates that the pathogenesis of MG-associated cognitive impairment involves complex central-peripheral interactions: mechanisms such as blood-brain barrier disruption, cross-reaction of specific autoantibodies, and neuroinflammatory responses can lead to direct CNS involvement, whereas chronic hypoxia (secondary to respiratory muscle weakness or sleep apnea), prolonged drug effects, and psychological factors like depression and anxiety associated with the disease may also indirectly impair cognitive function. Nevertheless, the field still faces numerous challenges, including the lack of large-scale longitudinal studies to elucidate the natural course and trajectory of cognitive impairment, as well as the identification of biomarkers. This narrative review collates recent research advances regarding MG-related cognitive impairment and discusses its clinical manifestations, confounding influencing factors, underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, and existing diagnostic difficulties.

C1.title: Chronic Post-Stroke Cognitive Impairment: Microglial Autophagy, PI3K/Akt/mTOR Signaling, and Persistent Neuroinflammation
C1.abstract: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a major contributor to long-term disability and reduced quality of life after ischemic stroke, yet the mechanisms operating during its chronic phase remain insufficiently integrated. Increasing evidence suggests that, beyond the acute insult, dysfunction of the neurovascular unit and the blood-brain barrier, systemic immune responses, secondary neurodegeneration in distal brain regions, white matter degeneration, and structural disconnection of neural networks may all contribute to the development of PSCI, and the pathological consequences of these processes may persist into the subsequent subacute and chronic phases. Persistent neuroinflammation may contribute to these pathological processes and promote cognitive decline. Dysregulation of microglial autophagy and the class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt)/mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signaling may represent candidate mechanisms underlying this persistent neuroinflammatory process. Under specific pathological conditions, sustained mTORC1 activity may promote inflammatory by inhibiting the initiation of autophagy and restricting the TFEB-dependent lysosomal transcriptional program, thereby impairing the clearance of damaged mitochondria and inflammation-related substrates. This sustained inflammatory state may disrupt neuronal and synaptic function and contribute to white matter injury and neural network dysfunction. We synthesize evidence related to persistent pathology following stroke and critically examine the interactions among PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling, microglial autophagy, and persistent neuroinflammation. Given the limited direct mechanistic evidence from chronic ischemic stroke, we also incorporate supportive findings from ischemia-related models and selected chronic neuroinflammatory conditions to build a more integrated mechanistic framework.

C1.title: Changes in neuroinflammatory and blood-brain barrier-related markers during methylphenidate treatment in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a prospective observational study
C1.abstract: This study aims to investigate within-participant changes in serum IL-6, S100B, and Claudin-5 levels during 3 months of methylphenidate treatment in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and to examine whether biomarker changes were associated with changes in ADHD symptom severity. This single-center, uncontrolled prospective observational study included 42 medication-naïve children aged 6-11 years with ADHD who completed 3 months of methylphenidate treatment. Serum IL-6, S100B, and Claudin-5 levels were measured at baseline and month 3. ADHD symptom severity was assessed using the Conners Parent Rating Scale-Revised: Short Form (CPRS-R:S) and the Conners Teacher Rating Scale-Revised: Short Form (CTRS-R:S). Associations between percentage changes in biomarkers and symptom scores were examined, with correction for multiple testing. Parent- and teacher-rated ADHD symptom severity decreased significantly over 3 months. Serum IL-6 and S100B levels also decreased significantly, whereas the change in Claudin-5 was not significant. A nominal inverse association was observed between percentage changes in IL-6 and teacher-rated symptom severity, but this association did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. Among children who completed the 3-month treatment period, methylphenidate was associated with reductions in selected peripheral biomarkers associated with inflammatory and glial processes. However, biomarker changes were not significantly associated with symptom changes after correction for multiple testing, and the uncontrolled observational design does not establish a causal effect of methylphenidate on these biomarkers. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07041333, registered on 19 June 2025. Prospectively registered. • Neuroinflammatory and blood-brain barrier-related alterations have been implicated in ADHD, but most available evidence is cross-sectional. • Longitudinal data on biomarker changes during methylphenidate treatment in medication-naïve children are limited. • Three months of methylphenidate treatment was accompanied by reductions in peripheral serum IL-6 and S100B, whereas Claudin-5 did not change significantly. • Within-participant biomarker changes were largely unrelated to symptom changes after correction for multiple testing.

C1.title: Esketamine Mitigates Perioperative Neurocognitive Impairment Through Attenuation of Blood-Brain Barrier Injury By Downregulating C3 Expression in Aged Mice
C1.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) are common complications in elderly patients, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a key contributing factor. This study investigated the effects of esketamine on postoperative cognitive function, BBB integrity, and complement component C3 (C3) expression in aged mice. Fifteen-month-old male C57BL/6 mice underwent laparotomy under sevoflurane anesthesia to establish a PND model. Animals were randomly assigned to five groups: control (CON), esketamine alone (ES), PND model (PND), PND with esketamine treatment (PND + ES), and PND with esketamine plus exogenous C3 (PND + ES + C3). Cognitive function was assessed using the Morris water maze and Y-maze tests. BBB permeability, ultrastructural alterations, and tight junction protein expression were evaluated in vivo by Evans Blue extravasation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Western blotting (WB), and immunofluorescence. In parallel, an in vitro BBB model using bEnd.3 cells was employed to examine the direct effects of esketamine on barrier function through measurements of transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and FITC-dextran permeability. Anesthesia and surgery induced significant early postoperative cognitive impairment in aged mice, accompanied by BBB disruption, decreased tight junction protein expression, and elevated C3 levels. Esketamine treatment alleviated cognitive deficits and attenuated BBB injury. Consistently, in vitro studies provided supportive evidence that esketamine enhanced barrier integrity in bEnd.3 cells. These protective effects were accompanied by reduced C3 and C3aR expression. Esketamine attenuated early postoperative cognitive impairment and BBB injury in aged mice, accompanied by reduced C3 expression. These findings suggest a possible contribution of C3-related processes, although the causal involvement of C3a-C3aR signaling remains to be established.

D2.title: Collapse of local circuit integrated information Φ during NREM sleep
D2.abstract: Clarifying the mechanisms underlying the emergence of consciousness remains a fundamental challenge in modern neuroscience. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) provides a mathematical framework derived from the phenomenological properties of consciousness as its axioms. IIT proposes that consciousness is identical to a system's intrinsic cause-effect information structure, quantified by integrated information Φ. While IIT predicts that the Φ of a neuronal system should decrease during the loss of consciousness, this hypothesis has remained untested at the neural circuit level. The present study provides empirical support for this IIT prediction. It was found that Φ within local circuits decreases during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep compared to wakefulness (and REM sleep in the frontal cortex), regardless of cortical laminar structure. The reduction in Φ was particularly pronounced during OFF-periods, when neural activity is collectively suppressed. These results align with IIT's framework, suggesting that the loss of consciousness corresponds to a collapse of integrated information within local circuits. The findings provide empirical support for IIT as a mathematical theory aiming to explain conscious experiences.

D2.title: System-level nonequivalence between integrated information and expected free energy in noisy permutation networks
D2.abstract: The free-energy principle (FEP) and active inference describe prediction and adaptation using generative models, whereas integrated information theory (IIT) examines intrinsic causal organization. Can knowledge of a network's prediction in its current state determine its intrinsic integration? We address this question using a fixed one-step state-risk expected free energy (EFE) and IIT system integrated information. Noisy binary permutation networks allow causal wiring to vary while local transition reliability remains fixed. From a homogeneous current state, different architectures have identical complete one-step predictive distributions, and thus identical EFE under common preferences and observation models. Nevertheless, multicycle architectures have zero whole-system IIT integration, while single cycles can be integrated. For an n-unit noisy single cycle with reliability η, we obtain the exact expression φsnη=min{2ηnlog22η,-nlog2η}. We prove that the minimum-information partition cuts exactly two causal edges, establish a unique interior maximum, and show that, in the large-n limit, the optimal reliability approaches unity, the joint specified-state probability approaches one half, and the maximum system integrated information approaches one ibit. Independent computation corroborates these results. Local surprisal-coordinate identities can be expressed through optimized variational free energy under exact inference, but this algebraic identity does not establish that a neural system performs variational inference. The counterexample establishes a state-conditioned non-identifiability limit for the specified EFE, not an incompatibility between IIT and the FEP. Bridging the two descriptions requires intervention-sensitive information beyond this single predictive distribution.

D2.title: Formalizing consciousness: a comparative mathematical analysis of leading theories
D2.abstract: This article provides a unified and accessible exposition of major mathematically articulated frameworks for consciousness: Integrated Information Theory (IIT), Global Workspace Theory (GWT), Active Inference (AIF), higher-order representation (HOR) approaches, and the Projective Consciousness Model (PCM). Building on probability theory, information theory, and geometric structures, we reformulate their core mechanisms in a shared mathematical language at the computational and algorithmic levels, following Marr's hierarchy. This enables rigorous comparison across theories that are often treated as conceptually incommensurable. Our analysis identifies shared formal tools, differences in explanatory scope, and specific questions for computational comparison. GWT emphasizes global availability; IIT emphasizes irreducible causal integration; Active Inference and HOR emphasize hierarchical inference and conscious access under uncertainty; PCM emphasizes the perspectival geometry of conscious experience. We assess computational tractability across frameworks and show that some apparent disagreements reflect differences in explanatory level rather than direct theoretical contradiction. We use this unified formal treatment to outline a route toward future computational comparisons: common testbed models in which integration, broadcasting, higher-order access, and perspectival transformations can be studied within the same agent architecture. The goal is to make overlaps, divergences, and empirical commitments across theories more explicit, thereby supporting more systematic model comparison in consciousness science.

D2.title: Protocol for measuring the effects of cortical scotoma on visual space perception
D2.abstract: We aim to investigate the spatial experience of patients with chronic scotomas caused by lesion to early visual cortex, including primary visual cortex (V1) and adjacent extrastriate visual areas. These experiments are conducted as part of an adversarial collaboration testing contrasting theories of consciousness: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and two Predictive Processing accounts, Active Inference (AI) and Neurorepresentationalism (NREP). The central question is whether lesions to early visual cortex alter the experienced extent of visual space itself, or instead primarily disrupt stimulus content within an otherwise preserved visual space. To address this, we use paradigms in which patients estimate distances or spatial extents that either span a scotomatous region or fall entirely within intact visual field locations. Psychometric functions relating perceived and physical extent are modeled to estimate shifts in the point of subjective equality (PSE). According to IIT, lesions to early visual cortex, including V1 and occipital extrastriate cortex, should lead to systematic reductions in perceived spatial extent across the scotoma (negative PSE shifts), reflecting a contraction of experienced space. In contrast, Predictive Processing accounts posit that higher-level predictive mechanisms preserve spatial structure despite loss of early input, predicting little or no systematic contraction (with NREP allowing limited context-dependent effects). By quantifying distortions in perceived spatial extent, this protocol aims to distinguish between these competing theoretical predictions.

D2.title: Kundalini phenomenology as expansion of perceptual capacity: a hypothesis and theory article integrating contemplative traditions and neuroscience
D2.abstract: Kundalini experiences-characterised by sensations of internal energy movement, sequential anatomical progression, boundary dissolution, and reports of expanded or cosmic consciousness-have been documented across contemplative traditions for millennia, yet remain theoretically underspecified within contemporary neuroscience. This paper proposes that these experiences can be understood, without metaphysical commitment, as reflecting a state-dependent expansion of perceptual capacity: the range and dimensionality across which an organism can apprehend patterns of integration, continuity, and coherence. The framework draws a distinction between perceptual capacity (what can be perceived) and perceptual content (what happens to be perceived at any moment), and argues that kundalini phenomenology maps onto progressive shifts from narrow, body-local, temporally fragmented perception toward multidimensional integrative awareness. The proposal is situated within three converging neuroscientific frameworks-global neuronal workspace theory, predictive processing, and network integration approaches-and is tested for structural consistency against liberation phenomenology across seven contemplative traditions: Śaiva/Tantric Hinduism, Pātañjala Yoga, Advaita Vedānta, Theravāda and Tibetan Buddhism, Daoism (neidan), Sufism (fanā/baqā), and Greek Stoicism. Where these traditions converge in describing a shift from positionally fixed to non-positionally witnessing consciousness, despite operating within substantially different cosmological and linguistic frameworks, the convergence constitutes evidence-not proof, but evidence-that a common phenomenological structure is being independently observed. The framework generates five falsifiable predictions, each specifying the measure, population, and expected direction of effect. It proposes that safety versus crisis outcomes in contemplative practice depend critically on the rate of perceptual expansion relative to individual integration capacity, and offers provisional clinical heuristics-explicitly labelled as hypotheses requiring prospective validation-for differential diagnosis between contemplative states and psychotic episodes. The present paper extends and complements the author's previously published neurophysiological model of kundalini, which proposed biomarker-level correspondences and a composite tracking metric (NDI); the present contribution addresses the phenomenological and perceptual-theoretic dimension that the earlier paper did not develop.

D2.title: The consciousness-first commitment of integrated information theory
D2.abstract: Integrated information theory (IIT) accounts for consciousness through its explanatory identity: an experience (the explanandum) is identical to a causal structure (or Φ-structure, the explanans). In other identities in science (e.g. 'water is H2O'), the power of the explanans (H2O) comes from the presumption that it somehow exists more fundamentally. Yet when our explanandum is experience itself, as in IIT, we must recalibrate the norms of explanation to the fact that experience exists immediately and irrefutably, while whatever we may posit about the world beyond experience is always an inference within experience.

D2.title: Spatial aspects of felt presence and the phenomenon of childhood imaginary companions: Peripersonal space, embodied perspective, and continuity of agent propensity
D2.abstract: Felt presence (FP), the sense that another agent is nearby without corresponding sensory evidence, occurs across neurological, psychiatric and non-clinical populations. Prior work links childhood imaginary companions (ICs) to anomalous and presence-related experience; we asked whether this link carries the spatial and perspectival signature predicted by a bodily self-consciousness (BSC) account. In 185 adults without psychiatric or neurological diagnoses (45 with and 140 without a childhood IC history), IC-positive participants retrospectively reported their companion's location, distance and perspective, and all participants completed the Sensed Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ) and a dissociation questionnaire. IC-positive adults scored significantly higher on the SenPQ, supporting the continuity prediction, whereas dissociation scores did not differ significantly between groups. Of the IC-positive participants, 88.9% (40 of 45) recalled their companion from a body-referenced (first-person or mixed first- and third-person) perspective. This offers tentative support for the perspective prediction, because three of the four response options were body-referenced. In 66.7% (76 of 114) of distance estimates for directions in which the companion had appeared, participants placed it within 70 cm of the body, our operational boundary of peripersonal space (PPS). This proportion significantly exceeded one half, offering moderate support for the peripersonal prediction. Companions were most often localized in front of and beside the body, unlike adult FP, which is typically experienced behind or beside the body. The findings provide partial evidence that the IC-presence link reflects the mechanisms proposed by a BSC account.

D2.title: A testable theoretical framework linking cranial osteopathic still-point induction to altered consciousness via convergent autonomic, default-mode, and interoceptive mechanisms
D2.abstract: Patients undergoing Still Point induction via compression of the fourth ventricle (CV4) in cranial osteopathy commonly report a distinctive quality of profound mental quiet, described as qualitatively different from ordinary relaxation. Cranial osteopathy, however, entered a prolonged crisis of scientific credibility once controlled work indicated that its founding construct, the Primary Respiratory Mechanism (PRM), could not be reliably palpated and that its proposed anatomical substrate, an inherent motility of the nervous system, palpable cranial bone motion, and a synchronised cranio-sacral rhythm, was not supported as originally formulated. In the absence of a defensible mechanism, the field has tended either toward vitalistic language or toward the untestable assertion that "something" therapeutic occurs. This paper does not defend the PRM. It proposes, instead, a modern and explicitly falsifiable theoretical framework: that CV4, treated as a standardisable manual procedure independent of the PRM construct, may transiently reconfigure a specific and measurable component of conscious experience, self-referential mental content, together with heightened interoceptive salience, through a convergent physiological cascade rather than through non-specific relaxation alone. We are explicit that "consciousness" here does not denote the global level or state of wakefulness, a brainstem-dependent arousal dimension, but a specific content dimension: the balance of self-referential versus present-moment, body-centred processing. The framework is assembled from convergent but indirect evidence drawn from autonomic, default-mode, interoceptive, and brain-state-clearance research; it therefore constitutes a chain of biological plausibility, not a demonstrated mechanism, and we say so throughout. Each proposed link is stated as a falsifiable prediction tested against a credible sham-touch comparator. We stress that the Default Mode Network (DMN) is used as a marker of one component of conscious content and is explicitly not treated as a proxy for consciousness itself. A dedicated section enumerates the non-specific alternatives, placebo and expectancy, generic effects of attentive touch, and demand characteristics, that any confirmatory study must exclude, and a further section concedes the framework's principal weakness: it lacks a firmly established grounding mechanism and, if not carefully specified and tested, risks relocating rather than resolving cranial osteopathy's long-standing problem of rational support. We set out what confirmation and what disconfirmation would each require the field to change in research, education, and integration into conventional care.

D2.title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential
D2.abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.
